headline: High risk of prompt injection, data leakage, and capability conflict from shared local-filesystem/MCP workflows between ctx and Windsurf.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ctx observes Claude Code events and uses MCP/stdio, while Windsurf exposes clipboard, workspace files, and MCP servers. That creates a plausible instruction-smuggling path through shared files or MCP content. The pair is not directly sandboxed together, so the interaction is inferred from documented surfaces rather than reproduced.
conditions: IF ctx reads Windsurf-authored workspace files as instructions
IF Windsurf forwards clipboard or MCP content into prompts without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable shared clipboard bridging between the two tools
Restrict both agents to separate workspaces
Add a provenance header check before parsing file content
Require manual review for any MCP-fed instructions
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and provenance tracking

B_data_leakage.rationale: Windsurf explicitly shares state via local filesystem and handles workspace files, while ctx touches filesystem and audit/runtime logs plus MCP servers. If both operate on the same workspace, ctx can ingest data Windsurf writes and vice versa, creating a realistic leakage path for source code, logs, or secrets. The default overlap is enough to treat this as dangerous.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same local workspace
IF either agent writes secrets or logs into shared files
mitigations: Use separate workspaces per agent
Exclude logs and secrets from shared directories
Turn off clipboard sharing
Rotate any secrets already present in the workspace
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ctx supports multiple instances and filesystem access, while Windsurf can write the filesystem, modify git state, and uses shared local filesystem state across instances. That combination creates a direct write-write conflict on the same repo or workspace, with possible git corruption or lost edits. The overlap is documented in both profiles, so uncertainty is low.
conditions: IF both agents edit the same git repository
IF either agent runs without external locking
mitigations: Pause one agent before the other writes
Use git worktrees or separate branches
Add a file-locking wrapper around writes
Review and reconcile diffs before commit
requires-engineering: implement orchestrator-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: ctx can observe tool events and Windsurf runs a single-agent loop with approval-per-command by default. If ctx-generated context or summaries are fed into Windsurf, Windsurf may act on them as authoritative without a verification step. The reverse path is also plausible through shared files, but the profiles do not prove automatic trust, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF ctx output is inserted into Windsurf prompts or files
IF Windsurf executes commands based on unverified ctx summaries
mitigations: Require a human verification step before execution
Mark ctx outputs as untrusted in prompts
Separate planning and execution workspaces
Add checksum or citation checks for handoffs
requires-engineering: add structured handoff validation

E_compliance.rationale: Windsurf is closed-source and handles model provider keys, while ctx is source-available and touches audit/runtime logs and harness records. If regulated or sensitive data is placed into the shared workspace, differing retention and logging behaviors could create a compliance mismatch. The profiles do not show a specific residency breach, so medium fits the documented uncertainty.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the shared workspace
IF retention or logging policies differ between the two tools
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces
Review vendor retention settings
Avoid storing secrets in logs
Document data-flow boundaries for both tools
requires-engineering: align retention and residency controls
